vignette:
Mai is a 71-year-old divorced woman of South Eastern Asian descent who works as a financial analyst. She came to therapy at the urging of her adult daughter, who had grown worried by the changes she had seen in her mother over the past three years. Mai did not argue with the referral, but she was not sure what talking could do. What frightened her most was not the memory itself but the feeling that she could no longer trust the world to operate the way it was supposed to.

The event that had shattered that trust occurred during a business trip to a regional office in another state. Mai had been sent to audit a subsidiary, and on her second night there, she was detained by two men who claimed to be security contractors for the company. They held her in a windowless conference room for nearly eighteen hours, accusing her of corporate espionage, threatening her with legal action, and refusing to let her leave or contact anyone. She was not physically harmed, but she was not allowed to use the bathroom without an escort, and she was made to sit in a hard chair facing a blank wall while the men argued on the phone with someone she never saw. She was finally released when the corporate legal team intervened, but no one ever apologized. The company offered a settlement in exchange for her silence, and when she refused to sign, her position was restructured into a less meaningful role. She had come to believe that the institutions that should have protected her—her employer, the local police who declined to investigate, the corporate ethics office that took six months to close the case with no findings—had all let her down in a coordinated, deliberate way.

In the months that followed, Mai found herself unable to stop thinking about how her life would have been different if that trip had never happened. She would lie awake at night, long past midnight, replaying the sequence of decisions that had led her to that conference room. If she had declined the assignment. If she had insisted on a different hotel. If she had called her daughter before the men arrived. She stayed up until two or three in the morning, sometimes later, because the moment she tried to sleep, the images would press in: the beige wall, the fluorescent hum, the way the men’s shoes squeaked on the linoleum. She tried hard not to think about it during the day, keeping herself busy with spreadsheets and quarterly reports, but her concentration had frayed. She made errors she had never made before, and her manager had begun to comment on her late submissions.

She had also developed a sharp, visceral sense that she was contaminated by what had happened. She showered twice a day, sometimes three times, and she had stopped wearing the blazer she had worn on that trip, even though it had been dry-cleaned. She felt dirty in a way that soap could not reach, and she was certain that other people could sense it. At work, she kept her desk turned so that her back was to the wall, and she had stopped eating lunch in the break room because the open space made her feel exposed. She only felt safe in her own apartment, and even there, she checked the locks on the windows three times before she could sit down. Night was worse. She found it harder to feel safe after dark, and she kept a small flashlight on her nightstand even though she knew rationally that no one was coming.

The consequences had accumulated quietly. She had stopped attending her weekly mahjong group because it met in a community center with large windows and too many entrances. She had declined invitations to her granddaughter’s school events because the crowds made her feel as though she might be trapped. Her daughter had noticed the withdrawal and had asked, gently, whether Mai was depressed. Mai did not think she was depressed. She thought she was broken in a different way. She could not deal with even the slightest upset anymore—a missed bus, a delayed email, a loud noise in the hallway—without feeling her heart race and her throat close. She had become a person who startled at nothing, and she hated that.

What finally brought her to the clinic was a panic attack in the office elevator. The doors had stuck for thirty seconds, and she had found herself unable to breathe, pounding on the metal, convinced that she would be trapped again. Her supervisor had called her daughter. Now Mai sat in the therapist’s office with her hands folded tightly in her lap, hoping that someone could help her sleep through the night again, but afraid that the only real solution would be to stop needing to trust anyone at all.
